Design and Performance Analysis of a 10-Bit Segmented Current-Steering DAC

Abstract:

Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) are essential components in modern communication systems, signal processing, and mixed-signal VLSI circuits. With the increasing demand for high-speed and low-power electronic devices, the design of high-performance DAC has become an important research area. Among various DAC architectures, Current-Steering DAC (CS-DAC) are widely preferred for high-speed applications due to their fast-switching capability and suitability for high sampling frequencies. However, achieving high linearity, low power consumption, and good dynamic performance simultaneously remains a significant challenge. The performance of CS-DAC is mainly affected by current-source mismatch, switching glitches, timing errors, and limited output impedance, which degrade Integral Nonlinearity (INL), Differential Nonlinearity (DNL), and Spurious-Free Dynamic Range (SFDR).

&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp In this work, an 8-bit segmented current-steering DAC has been designed and simulated using 180-nm CMOS technology. The architecture employs thermometer-coded current sources for the five most significant bits (MSB) and binary-weighted current sources for the three least significant bits (LSB). Retiming latches and a bias-generation circuit are incorporated to support synchronized switching and stable current generation. The simulation results demonstrate a maximum DNL of 0.446 LSB, INL of 0.722 LSB, and SFDR of 62.63 dB at a sampling frequency of 500 MS/s, with a power consumption of 3.18 mW. These results demonstrate satisfactory static linearity and dynamic performance.

The proposed research aims to extend the existing 8-bit architecture to a 10-bit segmented current-steering DAC in 180-nm CMOS technology. The main target is to improve the current source matching and output linearity by optimized current source structures, stable bias generation and suitable switching techniques. The proposed design will be evaluated in terms of INL, DNL, SFDR and power consumption in an effort to obtain a better compromise between linearity, speed and power efficiency.
